extracted.intended_audience: novelists, literary students, and critics interested in writing or evaluating fantasy and prophetic novels
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative criteria for composing and judging two major ‘aspects’ of the novel — fantasy (the fantastic) and prophecy (the prophetic/visionary tone). Focuses on reader demands, suitable devices, mythology, voice, style, and how those interact with character and plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader payment / willingness to accept the fantastic
rubrics_metrics.description: "So fantasy asks us to pay something extra." The fantastic requires an additional adjustment from the reader beyond ordinary realism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained via the sideshow metaphor: some readers "pay with delight" while others refuse with indignation. The criterion is whether the book’s fantastic demands are appropriate to its audience and whether it convinces readers to make that mental payment (example: Mr. Asquith willing to pay but hoping to get it back). Be mindful that fantasy can demand extra suspension of disbelief or emotional investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of fantastic elements to the book
rubrics_metrics.description: "Anything that suits it is true, so why should any question arise... except whether it is suitable to its book?" Fantastic elements must be judged by their fit within the work as an artistic entity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether introducing gods/angels/monsters or other supernatural devices coheres with the novel's internal laws and overall tone (example contrast between apparition and mortgage—both can be true inside fiction if suitable). Avoid incongruous insertions that break the book’s unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of supernatural or its absence (hedged requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: "They ask us to accept either the supernatural or its absence." A fantastic book typically asks the reader to accept a stance about the supernatural, but that stance may be expressed subtly or hedged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not over-define; some works (e.g., Tristram Shandy) suggest the supernatural without explicitly presenting it. Evaluate whether the text persuades readers toward acceptance or plausible ambiguity rather than forcing explicit supernatural mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: List and deployment of fantasy devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors of the fantastic commonly use devices such as "the introduction of a god, ghost, angel, monkey, monster, midget, witch into ordinary life; or the introduction of ordinary men into no man's land, the future, the past, the interior of the earth, the fourth dimension; or divings into and dividings of personality; or finally the device of parody or adaptation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the freshness and appropriateness of device use. The essay notes the set of devices is "strictly limited" but can be renewed by temperament and invention; beware of stale or mechanically repeated devices. Examples: Flecker’s Magic (witch and wish-ring), The Magic Flute (borrowed mythology), Ulysses (Odyssey mythology), Joseph Andrews (false-start parody).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvised air / beam-of-light focus characteristic of fantasy
rubrics_metrics.description: Fantasy novels often have "an improvised air, which is the secret of their force and charm," and a simile of a beam of light that "spotlights" objects that have no reason to anticipate it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the narrative retains an improvised, surprising quality (the "beam of light" effect) while still delivering coherent impressions; this improvisational quality contributes to the charm and must not be smothered by over-explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of realism, wit, charm, and mythology
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful fantasy often achieves "a mixture of realism, wittiness, charm and mythology," where mythology supports rather than overwhelms the work (example: Zuleika Dobson handled with this mixture).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the author balances mundane detail and comic/realistic elements with mythic or supernatural machinery. Beware two failure modes: mythology so heavy it makes the book laboured, or so thin it trivializes the fantasy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective use of parody and adaptation as mythology
rubrics_metrics.description: Parody or adaptation can be used "for his mythology some earlier work and uses it as a framework or quarry for his own purposes," providing inspiration, structure, and a ready-made pattern for writers who struggle to invent characters from scratch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the adaptation enriches the new work (e.g., Magic Flute → Lowes Dickinson; Odyssey → Ulysses) or degenerates into mere imitation or a 'false start' (example: Joseph Andrews beginning as parody but becoming a different novel). Good parody/adaptation should transform and repurpose its source, not simply lampoon it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merging magical and mundane language
rubrics_metrics.description: Technique: the fantasist "merge[s] the kingdoms of magic and common sense by using words that apply to both," enabling the mixture to come alive (Flecker example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate linguistic choices that allow phrases to mean both magical and ordinary things simultaneously; this semantic double-voicing helps integrate the fantastic into everyday perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character solidity within fantastic contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: "They may contain solid character-drawing, penetrating and bitter criticism of conduct and civilization; yet our simile of the beam of light must remain." Even in fantasy, characters can and should be well-drawn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether character depth and believable psychological detail are preserved despite—or enhanced by—the fantastic apparatus. Fantasy that reduces characters to mere types risks losing emotional grip.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintenance of tone through to the ending
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay warns that "towards the end—that dreadful end often so fatal to fiction—the book rather flags," illustrating that endings can fail to sustain the fantasy's promise (Zuleika’s ending and the mass suicide scene cited).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the novel sustains its invented tone and wit through its climax and resolution; endings should feel appropriate to the established mythology and tone, not collapse into awkwardness or bathos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophetic tone defined as an accent of voice
rubrics_metrics.description: "Prophecy—in our sense—is a tone of voice... His theme is the universe, or something universal... It is the implication that signifies and will filter into the turns of the novelist’s phrase." Prophetic fiction uses an elevated, singing voice that aspires to universality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the narrator/authorial voice for an elevated, song-like quality that treats events as instances of larger cosmic or moral significance. This tone will affect diction, rhythm, and the priority of ideas over mundane detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader qualities demanded by prophecy: humility and suspension of humour
rubrics_metrics.description: "The prophetic aspect demands two qualities: humility and the suspension of the sense of humour." Readers must lay aside ironic or comic distance to hear the prophet's voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the work requires and rewards a reader’s humility (willingness to take statements seriously) and temporary suspension of the sense of humour. If the voice is laughed at rather than accepted, the prophetic effect will fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality / symbolic extension of characters and events
rubrics_metrics.description: In prophetic fiction "the characters and situations always stand for more than themselves; infinity attends them... they expand to embrace it." Characters function as symbols pointing beyond their particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether characters and incidents are organically extended to suggest universal ideas (as in Dostoevsky) rather than merely coinciding with moral sermonizing (contrast with George Eliot). Beware works that merely preach without achieving symbolic extension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to minutiae of style for prophetic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: For prophecy the critic notes "we shall come nearer than elsewhere to the minutiz[e] of style... we shall have to attend to the novelist’s state of mind and to the actual words he uses; we shall neglect as far as we can the problems of common sense."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate sentence-level and diction-level choices—phrasing, rhythm, metaphor—that produce the prophetic resonance. Style here is not ornament but vehicle of implication; judge whether wording carries the required extension of meaning rather than collapsing into affectation.
